item.title: Dutch government is neglecting Bonaire climate change ruling
item.description:
Dutch government is neglecting Bonaire climate change ruling

July 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The government is not taking measures to address its legal obligations to protect the former Dutch colony of Bonaire from the ravages of climate change, according to an investigation by NOS.

A court in The Hague ruled in January the government had acted in a discriminatory manner towards Bonaire by excluding the Caribbean island from its climate plans.

Although the cabinet has appealed, ministers are still obliged to comply with the terms of the judgment, including providing an assessment of how much greenhouse gas that the Netherlands believes it can still emit without exceeding the Paris climate goals.

That report was due today and, according to the NOS, the government has not submitted it.

“Failing to provide insight into that scope is simply negligent,” climate lawyer Laura Burgers of the University of Amsterdam told NOS.

In response to questions from the broadcaster, climate minister Stientje van Veldhoven-van der Meer said that the cabinet will provide more information on Budget Day – 15 September – regarding how the Bonaire ruling will be implemented.

Eight people from the Caribbean island of Bonaire joined forces with environmental organisation Greenpeace to sue the Dutch government for failing to protect them against climate change.

item.title: Vandals attack homes as row over asylum seekers turns violent
item.description:
Vandals attack homes as row over asylum seekers turns violent

July 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A bitter war has broken out in two Brabant villages over plans to accommodate 50 refugees in the area, with supporters having their homes vandalised by anti-immigration campaigners.

Slogans using words such as teef (bitch) and hoer (whore) were scrawled on the walls and windows of homes in Bokhoven and Engelen, near Den Bosch, where the council’s plans have been the focus of heated protests and riots.

One couple, who gave their names as Rob and Ingrid, told Omroep Brabant they were not outright supporters of the plan, but had called for an open debate about the implications.

“We understand that people in De Vutter [the location of the proposed shelter] have real concerns,” Rob said.

He accused opponents of the scheme of trying to shut down the discussion through intimidation and violence. “A few months ago Ingrid called in our village newspaper for us to stand together as a village and organise things properly,” he said.

“That open approach has meant that the media and others have put us on the side of the actual supporters and our name has been circulated by extreme opponents.”

Spreading law

The municipality announced in April it wanted to house 50 boys and girls aged between 15 and 18 on an industrial site in the area, to meet its obligations under the so-called “spreading law” that requires councils to share the responsibility for accommodating asylum seekers.

Demonstrations that were held outside community meetings turned to riots as stones were thrown and fireworks were let off.

Police in riot gear with dogs cleared away a group of 100 protesters, some of whom tried to block the A59 motorway, and arrested two people during two nights of violence.

In May the council announced it was postponing the decision so it could hold more community information sessions. Two days later an explosion damaged the building where the refugees were due to be held.

Rob said it was clear from camera footage that the attacks on his home had been carried out by a group of youths.

“Once the police have caught the youths, we would like to have a conversation with them,” he said. “They probably have no idea how it affects you emotionally when you go through this.”

Syrians attacked

In a separate incident, police in Geesteren said a family of asylum seekers from Syria had been targeted several times by vandals and had their car set on fire after moving in to the village earlier this year.

The family, whose children are aged six, three and one, were allocated the house after being granted settled status, four years after they first arrived in the Netherlands.

Windows in the property have been smashed three times since March and on Sunday night their car was set ablaze. Police are treating the incident as arson, but say locals are too anxious to come forward with information.

Community silence

“The anxiety means people don’t dare to talk to us,” local police spokeswoman Chantal Westerhoff told NOS. “What I mean by that is that we have no tips at present or indications of who caused this.”

The mayor of Tubbergen, Anko Postma, whose municipality includes Geesteren, said extra protection was being arranged for the family.

“This must have a big impact on a family just as they are trying to build a new life here,” he said. “We are in contact with them and are looking at what support they need.”

The father, Al Arab, told NOS he was considering leaving the village because he was worried his family were becoming a burden. “Maybe it’s better if we go. Our dear neighbours are getting scared,” he said.

item.title: Four Dutch tourists found after speedboat goes missing in Malawi
item.description:
Four Dutch tourists found after speedboat goes missing in Malawi

July 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Four Dutch tourists who were reported missing when a speedboat failed to return from a trip on Lake Malawi have been found safe.

Malawian authorities put out an alert after the Tanzanian-registered boat failed to arrive at the expected time at Nkhata Bay on Sunday.

Three crew members, two from Malawi and one from Tanzania, were also on board, but there had been no contact from the vessel since it left Mbamba Bay, on the Tanzanian side of the lake, between 10am and 11am.

The Dutch foreign affairs ministry said the visitors were safely on land and had been given medical assistance, but did not give any further details of their condition, citing privacy concerns.

“Thanks to the search operation by the local authorities, in co-operation with the embassy, this worrying situation has thankfully been concluded.”

The speedboat belonged to a Tanzanian businessman, who alerted the authorities when he was unable to contact the crew and visitors on board, local news site the Nyasa Times reported.

Boats crossing the lake are required to register their arrival time with the port master 24 hours in advance, but this protocol was not followed. Local fishermen, boat operators and lakeshore communities were all urged to look out for the missing vessel during the search operation.

item.title: Prince Bernhard cashes out of real estate to go into AI
item.description:
Prince Bernhard cashes out of real estate to go into AI

July 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prince Bernhard has sold his entire business portfolio, including his stake in the Zandvoort motor racing circuit, and will now focus on AI.

The first cousin of king Willem-Alexander told Dutch press agency ANP that he was selling his interest in Media Park in Hilversum, IT company Levi9, and his extensive real estate portfolio to his business partners.

“The world is changing faster than ever. New technologies, artificial intelligence, and major societal changes are creating opportunities that we could hardly have imagined ten years ago,” he said.

The 56-year-old did not disclose the amount of the sale, but business magazine Quote has estimated his net worth at around €160 million.

Bernhard’s large real estate holdings – 98 buildings according to Quote – have earned him the nickname pandjesprins, or the property prince.

In 2017, an investigation by Amsterdam newspaper Het Parool found that Bernhard’s companies engaged in practices that violated Amsterdam’s housing regulations.

Earlier this year, Bernhard announced he and his wife, Princess Annette, were separating after 25 years of marriage.

The prince bought the Zandvoort circuit 10 years ago with the aim of bringing Formula 1 back to the Netherlands. F1 racing returned to Zandvoort in 2021 after a 36-year absence, after the scheduled 2020 race was cancelled because of the coronavirus pandemic.

The final edition of the Dutch Grand Prix will be held later this year. Organisers announced in 2024 that they wouldn’t continue beyond the current contract because the costs were too high.

item.title: Manhunt launched after Dutch man found strangled in German hotel
item.description:
Manhunt launched after Dutch man found strangled in German hotel

July 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

German police are urgently trying to trace the travel companion of a Dutch tourist who was found strangled in a hotel room close to the border.

The 35-year-old victim was discovered by staff on Sunday at Hotel Rheinpark in Rees, a German town about 30km south of Doetinchem.

A postmortem examination confirmed that the man had been strangled. He checked in to the hotel with another man on Saturday evening, but only the victim’s details were recorded in the guest register.

A murder inquiry was launched and forensic researchers spent several hours examining the room after the body was found at around noon, after the two guests failed to check out on time.

German media said the pair arrived on Saturday in a Dutch-registered car from the Enschede area.

Police are treating the man who checked in to the hotel room with the victim as the main suspect and have launched an urgent appeal to find him. They are also studying camera footage and trying to trace the two men’s route through phone data.

item.title: Sinking foundations could trigger €54bn housing repair bill
item.description:
Sinking foundations could trigger €54bn housing repair bill

July 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

More than 400,000 buildings in the Netherlands have problems with their foundations or are likely to develop them in the next 10 years, a government watchdog has warned.

Buildings are sinking for a combination of reasons, including falling groundwater levels, bacterial erosion, drought, structural faults and the impact of construction work. Earthquakes caused by gas drilling in Groningen have also destabilised houses in the northern province.

In around 120,000 cases the buildings are in urgent need of repair, the council for the environment and infrastructure (Rli) concluded in a report. If nothing is done the cost of repairing the damage could add up to €54 billion.

The problems have been made worse by the impact of climate change, Mandy Korff, foundations expert at the TU Delft university told Nu.nl. “If the groundwater level drops, whether through human activity or climate change, the ground level sinks and houses without foundation piles sink with it.”

Housing shortage

The Rli has called for new housing developments to be built on land that is solid enough to bear the load, but that will make it even more challenging to meet the government’s target of 100,000 new homes a year, which is one of the cabinet’s main priorities.

“Shortage of space is connected to the choices we make about accessibility, agriculture and where we need to build houses based on where people want to live,” Korff said.

Since April surveyors have been obliged to include details of the state of the foundations in homebuyers’ reports. Tamara Evers of SVn, a non-profit organisation that arranges loans for sustainable housing repairs, said the move was a step in the right direction, but foundation problems were not always visible.

She also questioned if homeowners should bear the responslbility for the repairws alone. “Some can afford to repair their homes, others can’t, and the question is whether if is fair to leave it to the individual homeowner when you consider all the different underlying causes.”

item.title: Two youths come forward over assault during Nijmegen Vierdaagse
item.description:
Two youths come forward over assault during Nijmegen Vierdaagse

July 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Two teenage boys have handed themselves in to police after a security guard was assaulted during last week’s four-day Vierdaagse walking festival in Nijmegen.

The guard suffered serious injuries when he was punched and kicked at a bicycle parking lot in Nijmegen’s Stationsplein during the night of Tuesday to Wednesday, police said.

Police said at least four people were involved in the assault and released photographs of the suspects with their faces blurred. They warned that their faces would be revealed if they did not come forward within a week.

The photographs of the two youths who came forward have since been taken offline.

No details were disclosed about what might have led to the attack.

It is one of several incidents to take place during this year’s Vierdaagse, the annual walking festival around the Gelderland city.

An 18-year-old man from Rotterdam was arrested on Wednesday on suspicion of assaulting another man at the weekend.

Fatal shooting

On Saturday evening four teenagers and a 19-year-old youth were arrested for allegedly assaulting a girl on Molenstraat, while police also had to deal with a fight that broke out at a pavement café in Bloemerstraat in which tables and chairs were thrown.

On Tuesday night an 18-year-old man, also from Rotterdam, was fatally shot on Graafsweg, close to the festivities. He died of his injuries in hospital despite the efforts of paramedics and an air ambulance crew to resuscitate him.

Another 18-year-old man was arrested in connection with the shooting, which police said was not directly linked to the Vierdaagse events.

The city council stepped up security around the festival in response to the incidents by restricting the number of visitors and authorising police to carry out preventive stop-and-search checks.

item.title: What books to take for your summer holiday
item.description:
What books to take for your summer holiday

July 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Are you getting ready for your summer holidays and trying to decide which book to take to read on the beach? We’ve got some suggestions for you.

Summer House with a Swimming Pool
Not to be too on the nose, but the book by famed Dutch writer Herman Koch is the perfect book for your beach bag. It brings together all of Koch’s best: unlikeable characters, an unreliable narrator, a page-turning plot and the complicated relationships between parents and children. Plus, it’s literally set during a summer holiday.

A disturbing summer holiday: Summer House With A Swimming Pool

Death on a Tiny Scale
The book follows the bumbling Tony Solano, a technical writer in London, as he travels abroad to close down the office he’s inherited from an unknown party. He hires a temporary assistant to help with the administration, as the Brit doesn’t speak a word of Dutch and is now faced with a lease, case files and an inadvertently adopted a cat. If you liked it, a second in the series has already been published and author Julie Broussely, a Brit who relocated to the Netherlands, is underway with the third.

Death on a Tiny Scale: a fun mystery with some small problems

The Ghost Ship
Want some romance with your pina colada? The Ghost Ship starts in the gallows, ends in the gallows and in between has swashbuckling lady pirates, forbidden romance and 16th century Amsterdam. Author Kate Mosse, widely known for her archaeological fiction novel Labyrinth, is the author of more than 10 historical fiction books.

Pirates, romance and a history lesson: The Ghost Ship

Bearer of Bad News
Going to the mountains instead of to the beach? Follow the adventures of mediocre hairdresser Lucy Rey just stumbled across the perfect wanted ad that will free her from a job she hates and a cheating boyfriend, or is there more to this post that has turned up on her social media feed? The book follows Rey from a miserable life in Las Vegas on an unexpected journey to the Italian mountains, where she’s been offered a job that seems too good to be true and turns out to be much more complicated and personal than she ever expected.

Bearer of Bad News: a quirky and funny read

The Goldfinch
If you are going to insist on something that will impress those passing by your cabana, The Goldfinch is the way to go. Donna Tartt, of The Secret History fame, partially sets her third novel in the Netherlands and the titular painting is a Dutch classic that (in real life) hangs in the Mauritshuis. The book follows 13-year old Theo Dekker as he survives a terrorist attack, steals the priceless art work and ends up in a hotel room in Amsterdam more than a decade later.

The Goldfinch: A hefty classic that is worth its weight in gold

The Diary Keepers
If you are one of those people who wants to learn something while you’re on holiday, author Nina Siegal dived into more than 2,000 personal diaries kept by the Dutch during World War II, combining excerpts to create a compelling day-by-day narrative of the Holocaust in the Netherlands. The book splices together a vivid account, sometimes presenting differing views of the same event, of a near-daily record of the war.

The Diary Keepers: eyewitness accounts of World War II

item.title: Inspectors criticise use of armed wardens to escort refugees
item.description:
Inspectors criticise use of armed wardens to escort refugees

July 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The agency responsible for transporting failed asylum seekers has been strongly reprimanded for letting civilian wardens carry guns while escorting a group of refugees to a deportation flight.

The prisoner transport service DV&O “deliberately” exceeded its powers by using armed wardens (boa’s) when it had no authority to do so, justice ministry inspectors wrote in their annual report.

The guards accompanied 83 Syrian nationals who were being deported to Damascus on a government-chartered flight in September last year.

It was the first mass deportation flight to be arranged under a voluntary scheme for Syrians, who receive a one-way ticket and €1,000 in cash if they agree to drop their claim for asylum irrevocably. The wardens were deployed as security for the group and to protect the cash reserves.

The DV&O’s illegal use of civilian wardens, rather than military police, “put its staff in a vulnerable position” because they were not authorised to use their weapons while travelling with the detainees.

“They could have been held personally liable if they had had to use force in the execution of their duties,” the inspectorate said.

Second infringement

The flight was arranged by the repatriation service DTenV, but the transfer of refugees to the airport was the responsibility of the DV&O. In all other respects the flight complied with the rules on deporting refugees, the inspectors said.

The report is published at a sensitive time for asylum minister Bart van den Brink, who wants to extend the powers of civilian wardens to deal with disruptive and rejected asylum seekers.

It is not the first time the transport service has been criticised for using armed wardens without authorisation to supervise refugees.

Three years ago the inspectorate found they were being used to enforce detention rules in the high-security refugee centre in Hoogeveen even though there was no legal basis for deploying them.

In its response to the report, the DV&O questioned why the inspectors had referred to the previous incident in a footnote.

The inspectorate replied that it had included the reference to explain why it took a “very serious” view of the most recent incident.

item.title: Ageing population puts pressure on Dutch dental care providers
item.description:
Ageing population puts pressure on Dutch dental care providers

July 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

New research by Rabobank shows that the country’s ageing population is putting increasing pressure on dental care providers.

A report published on Monday warns there are not enough dentists too keep up with the specialsed needs of the elderly.

“The increasing ageing of the population also brings with it changing challenges in terms of knowledge and the way of working in dental practices,” the report says.

In 2045, more than one in seven residents of the Netherlands will be older than 75, compared to one in ten now.

The proportion of people over 75 without their own teeth has fallen considerably in the last two decades, thanks to technological advancements and the improved financial situation for many later in life. As such, older people often need more frequent and specialised care including the maintenance of crowns, bridges and implants.

People over 75 contacted the dentist 3.2 times a year on average in 2025, compared to 1.6 times in 2014, the report says.

More capacity needed

The professional association KNMT warned parliament in 2021 that a shortage of service providers was looming and called for more capacity to train dentists.

Currently, there are 259 dental training places at three universities. Last year, the education ministry decided to gradually expand the number of dentistry study places to 290 by 2027.

The gaps are already being filled by dentists from other countries. Some 25 percent of the dentists working in the Netherlands were trained abroad and that number continues to rise.
